position: Monetary Rule Reform Options; Minimum Effective Reforms
proposal: The chapter recommends taking monetary discretion away from the Federal Reserve through free banking, commodity-backed money or a strict policy rule, presenting options in decreasing order of effectiveness: free banking, commodity-backed money, a K-percent money growth rule, inflation targeting, and inflation and growth targeting such as NGDP targeting or a Taylor rule (pp. 735-740). It says a K-percent rule may be the most feasible option and that the choice should ultimately be made through the lawmaking process (p. 740).
remaining: Any statutory monetary rule, commodity backing or free banking
Statement of an inflation target range by elected officials (tracked in c24-01)

status_summary: No bill establishing free banking, commodity-backed money, a K-percent rule or another statutory policy rule was found in the 119th Congress. The FOMC's Statement on Longer-Run Goals and Monetary Policy Strategy, revised 2025-08-22 and reaffirmed unchanged on 2026-01-28, keeps a 2 percent inflation goal, names the federal funds rate as the primary policy tool, contains no averaging language and references no policy or money growth rule. The gold-related bills seen (H.R. 3795 and S. 3218, Gold Reserve Transparency Act of 2025) concern reserve transparency, not a gold standard. A different measure, H.R. 5396 (Price Stability Act of 2026), would remove maximum employment from the goals of monetary policy and sets no rule, commodity standard or free banking; the House Financial Services Committee ordered it reported on 2026-05-13 and reported it on 2026-06-24 (H. Rept. 119-710), and its status record shows no floor action.

timeline.event: The FOMC released a revised Statement on Longer-Run Goals and Monetary Policy Strategy that keeps the 2 percent goal, drops averaging language and adopts no policy rule.
The FOMC reaffirmed the statement, identical to the August 2025 version, with no policy rule.

title: Replace discretionary Fed policy with a monetary rule, such as a K-percent rule
uncertainties: No bill establishing free banking, commodity-backed money, a K-percent rule or another statutory policy rule was found. An external retrieval of Congress.gov and web searches (22 queries, run 2026-10-22; it cannot be reproduced here) covered K-percent and Taylor-type rule bills, the dual mandate, gold or commodity standards and free banking in the 119th Congress, and found one related bill: H.R. 5396, which would remove maximum employment from the statutory goals of monetary policy. Its status record, opened on govinfo.gov, shows it ordered reported 30 to 21 on 2026-05-13, reported on 2026-06-24 and placed on the Union Calendar, and not law; it imposes no rule on the conduct of policy, so it is treated as related and does not move the stage. The external retrieval excluded the Gold Reserve Transparency Act bills (H.R. 3795, S. 3218), bills to abolish the Federal Reserve Board (H.R. 1846, S. 869) and H.R. 4975 (a removal procedure for the Chairman tied to benchmarks) as not matching; these were not opened, and H.R. 3795 and S. 3218 were seen only on tracker pages. It also found no Federal Reserve adoption of such a rule. The FOMC statement revised 2025-08-22 and reaffirmed 2026-01-28 references no policy or money growth rule; the 2025-08-22 release page itself does not print the statement text. The Federal Reserve Unified Agenda rule list on reginfo.gov (headed 'Agency Rule List - 2026', 13 rules) lists no monetary rule entry; strategy is set by statement or statute, so the agenda is a weak test. The congress.gov search could not be opened here, so a bill under another name remains possible. Checked systematically on 2026-10-19; external retrieval results added 2026-10-22.
